papers.title: Two Timescales of Forgetting in Fine-tuning of Language Models: Fast Behavioral Suppression and Slow Representational Drift
papers.abstract: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.

papers.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
papers.abstract: The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory. To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner. We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.

papers.title: Correlation-Aware Evidential Fusion for Trusted Multi-View Classification
papers.abstract: Trusted multi-view classification aims to make accurate and reliable predictions by integrating information from multiple views. Existing methods typically estimate class evidence and uncertainty for each view and combine the resulting opinions through aggregation rules. However, they generally treat different views as independent information sources, overlooking the correlations among them. Highly correlated views tend to produce similar evidence, and treating them as independent sources may repeatedly count consistent information and give it disproportionate influence, while weakening complementary evidence that provides additional information. Consequently, such correlation-unaware fusion may not only limit classification performance but also produce miscalibrated uncertainty estimates. To address this issue, we propose Correlation-Aware Fusion of Evidence (CAFE), a framework for trusted multi-view classification. CAFE applies complementarity-based trust discounting to the evidence produced by view-private experts and introduces a correlation-aware constraint to reduce the repeated contribution of similar evidence. It then learns sample-specific weights from the global multi-view context to adaptively combine the correlation-adjusted private evidence with cross-view collaborative evidence. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that CAFE consistently improves classification and calibration performance in general settings, with particularly significant gains when strong correlations exist among views.

papers.title: Fixed Points and Envelope Dynamics on Credal Hyperspaces
papers.abstract: Let $X$ be a compact metric space and consider the hyperspace $\mathscr C_X$ of nonempty weakly closed convex sets of Borel probability measures on $X$, called credal sets. These sets represent uncertainty about which probability law governs the phenomenon of interest. We equip $\mathscr C_X$ with the Hausdorff metric induced by a metric for weak convergence. Credal order intervals $[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}] = \{ \mathcal{P}\in\mathscr C_X: \mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{B} \}$ are complete lattices, and every inclusion-monotone, Hausdorff-continuous self map of such an interval has least and greatest fixed points obtained as limits of iteration from $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$. For families of inclusion-monotone updates that may vary with time, we construct lower and upper envelope maps that bound every admissible trajectory. When these envelope maps are Hausdorff-continuous, the distance of every trajectory from a limiting credal interval vanishes uniformly over all switching sequences and initial credal sets. Coalescence of the limiting interval endpoints yields convergence to a common credal limit. We then construct the credal evolution induced by a time consistent Nisio semigroup. Uniform $W_1$ contraction of the underlying Markov semigroups induces Hausdorff-Wasserstein contraction of the credal evolution, yielding a unique common invariant credal set, exponential convergence from every initial credal set, and a support functional equal to the robust ergodic limit. We also derive perturbation bounds from finite time Nisio discrepancies and one step kernel set discrepancies, and characterize the countable sequences of support coordinates that represent credal sets, providing an explicit reconstruction formula.

papers.title: Human-Centered Learning Mechanics: Observable Entropy Control under Protected-Risk Constraints
papers.abstract: Human-Centered Learning Mechanics (HCLM) treats learning as an open, controlled process in which task progress, representation information, structural restrictions and externally specified risk limits jointly govern parameter updates. We characterise this mechanism through a normalised covariance-information force, metric observability and exact feasible rate constraints. The projected task rate depends on an observable cross-product that differs from the ordinary task information product when a probe set does not contain the training task. Error, finite-step and delay margins specify when admissible local requests can be implemented. A primary 288-run neural study separates information control from empirical risk protection and retains cases where extra compression worsens held-out loss. Follow-up experiments train the observable restriction in a declared 13-dimensional subspace, implement a frozen-public-encoder readout through an actual Gaussian sample channel, evaluate a fixed-coefficient sensitivity grid, and test targeted nuisance control with two-hidden-layer minibatch learning on Fashion-MNIST. The nuisance study improves shifted accuracy over ERM, while generic protected balancing accounts for most of the gain. Together, the theory and experiments identify attainable information actions, predictive costs and the separate assumptions required for population-risk certification.

papers.title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning Under a Generative Model
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning is a subfield of machine learning that studies how an agent interacts with an environment in order to extract as large a reward as possible. A standard approach to study such interaction is through Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and the task of choosing an optimal policy---a function that tells the agent which action to take. In this work, we study two types of time-dependent MDP---finite-horizon and infinite-horizon discounted---and propose new quantum algorithms for computing approximate optimal policies. Our quantum algorithms are based on a new combination of standard value iteration and quantum subroutines like quantum mean estimation and quantum maximum finding, overall enhanced with techniques from sample-optimal classical algorithms. Our resulting query complexities improve upon previous works, thus approaching already established quantum lower bounds.

papers.title: Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization Beyond $1/e$ with Feasible Gradient Queries
papers.abstract: We study adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets $K\subseteq[0,1]^d$ when gradients may be queried only at feasible points. The online approximation coefficients $4/9$ (Aggarwal and Lu) and $2\sqrt{3}-3\approx 0.4641$ (Aggarwal and Du) rely on queries along chains that start from the all-ones vector and leave $K$. With every query in $K$, the best known coefficient was $1/e$. We give an online algorithm with coefficient $0.4013$ that, in each round, plays a random action, queries one gradient at a point of $K$, and makes one projection. Its expected approximate regret is $O(RB(1+R)\sqrt{T})$, where $R\le\sqrt{d}$ bounds the norm of points of $K$ and $B$ bounds the gradient norm on $K$. For a budget $\sum_i x_i\le k$, the bound is $O(kB\sqrt{T})$. The algorithm keeps a state $x\in K$, and the analysis applies the coordinate-chain comparison of Aggarwal and Lu inside the box $[0,x]$, which keeps every query feasible. A second comparison, along a path from $0$ in the direction $x$, cancels the extra terms that the box creates. Because the queries are feasible, they can be played, which gives regret $O(T^{2/3})$ under semi-bandit feedback and $O(T^{4/5})$ under bandit feedback with bounded values. Unbiased stochastic gradients with bounded second moment keep the $\sqrt{T}$ rate, and on a fixed function the algorithm attains $0.4013\,\mathrm{OPT}-\varepsilon$ in expectation with $O(1+R^2(1+R)^2B^2/\varepsilon^2)$ feasible gradient queries.

papers.title: Differentially Private Policy Optimization in Linear MDPs with Adversarial Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in personalized services often relies on sensitive interaction data. Motivated by the need to protect these data, we study differentially private (DP) policy optimization in episodic linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with unknown transitions and adaptive adversarial linear rewards under full-information feedback. This setting poses two key challenges: past trajectories are repeatedly reused for policy evaluation, and reward choices may depend on previously released private statistics. The proposed algorithm combines batched proximal policy optimization (PPO) updates with optimistic policy evaluation, using private regression statistics and reward estimates to protect both trajectories and reward functions under joint differential privacy (JDP). With all other parameters fixed, our high-probability regret bound retains the same leading $\widetilde{O}\left(K^{3/4}\right)$ dependence on the number of episodes $K$ as the corresponding non-private bound for batched optimistic PPO. The additional privacy terms scale as $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{5/8}\right)$ and $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{1/2}\right)$. Thus, privacy incurs only lower-order additive costs in $K$, even under adaptive adversarial rewards.

papers.title: Amortizing Exact Orthogonality: Drift-Triggered Restoration for Orthogonal Fine-Tuning
authors: Xiaoyu Li (University of New South Wales)
papers.abstract: Orthogonal finetuning (OFT) adapts a pretrained weight by an orthogonal transform and preserves its singular values and row angles, but existing methods construct an exact or approximate orthogonal transform at every optimization step. We measure how far a transform $A$ is from orthogonal by its orthogonality defect $\|A^\top A-I\|_2$. For OFTv2, which truncates a Cayley-Neumann series, we show that the truncation order does not determine the defect. At its default order, block defects in checkpoints from the reference implementation span five orders of magnitude. We propose Restarted Tangent Orthogonal Finetuning (RTOFT), which uses the first-order update $W(I+S)$ of a weight $W$ with a skew-symmetric $S$ and restores exact orthogonality by a polar decomposition only when the drift $\|S\|_2$ reaches a tolerance $\tau$. The defect of $I+S$ is exactly $\|S\|_2^2$. Therefore, reading the drift after every update and restoring before the next forward pass guarantees a defect of at most $\tau^2$ in every forward pass, independently of the loss, data, model, and optimizer. A final restoration makes the returned transform exactly orthogonal. On GLUE, RTOFT reduces the training time of block-diagonal, subspace, and butterfly parameterizations from $1.10$-$1.58\times$ to $0.97$-$1.13\times$ that of LoRA, and its block-diagonal version exceeds LoRA by $1.98\pm0.39$ points on the six-task average over five seeds. At $\tau=0.10$, the largest drift read during training stays between $0.10$ and $0.12$ across DeBERTaV3, Qwen, and diffusion models, whereas it ranges from $0.17$ to $1.65$ when restoring once per epoch. In all seven settings of our ablation, the tangent update is worse without restoration than with it, and restoring after every step yields no measurable accuracy gain over restoring at the tolerance and costs $4.5$-$27.5\%$ more per step.

papers.title: CondUQ: Calibrated Conditional Uncertainty Quantification Using Distribution Matching
papers.abstract: Many applications, especially reliability- and safety-critical ones, require accurate uncertainty quantification for the outputs of model- or learning-based measurement, estimation, and prediction systems. The errors of such systems often vary with factors such as input quality and operating conditions, and thus cannot be accurately described by a single Gaussian model. Although Gaussian mixture models and calibrated quantiles can approximate such error distributions, their unconditional forms do not capture how the error behavior depends on these factors. Hence, we propose condUQ, an approach that conditions error models on observable factors for enabling accurate and reliable uncertainty quantification. condUQ is built on top of an existing system without modifying it and applies even when the system is a black box. First, condUQ maps the observable factors to a latent quality index (QI) such that errors sharing the same QI follow a common, approximately Gaussian conditional distribution. The QI predictor is trained end-to-end with a distribution-matching objective, without requiring quality labels. Second, for each QI, a Gaussian error model is then fitted and calibrated on a large held-out dataset. condUQ is demonstrated on three examples: (a) GPS multipath errors conditioned on satellite elevation and signal strength, (b) relative attitude errors of a transformer-based visual relative pose regression model conditioned on its internal features of the image pairs, and (c) prediction errors of a world model conditioned on the input observations and actions. In all three examples, condUQ substantially reduces the discrepancy between the modeled and empirical error distributions compared with a single global model. Moreover, the learned QIs reveal how the underlying factors affect the error characteristics in a manner consistent with physical principles.

papers.title: BReD: Block Replay Dithering for Stable Low-Bit EMA Optimizer States
papers.abstract: Low-bit storage of optimizer states can substantially reduce the memory footprint of large-scale training. In practice, however, these states are not quantized once: at every training step, they are dequantized, updated, requantized, and written back. This iterative quantization pipeline can destabilize training. We identify a failure mode behind this instability: for states updated via exponential moving averages (EMAs), quantization errors are recursively fed into subsequent updates. As a result, biased errors accumulate over time while high-variance errors are amplified, particularly when the EMA decay factor is close to 1. To address this error accumulation, we propose BReD (Block Replay Dithering), a method that reduces rounding bias and controls rounding variance during quantization. BReD adapts classical subtractive dithering to optimizer-state quantization by combining deterministic seed replay with block-wise shared dither values, avoiding auxiliary random-tensor storage and per-element dither values generation. Across the default pretraining settings (five optimizers at 120M; AdamW and Muon at 1.1B and 3.4B model) and supervised fine-tuning (AdamW and Muon at 7B model), 4-bit BReD closely matches training with full-precision optimizer states, with PPL shifts $\leq0.5$ in pretraining and $\leq0.2$ in fine-tuning and average downstream performance changes within 0.7 points. Moreover, 3-bit BReD preserves stable convergence in the evaluated settings, offering a more aggressive alternative. Our implementation of BReD is available at: https://github.com/ZhanHeshen/BReD

papers.title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
papers.abstract: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $\pi_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $\mu_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.

papers.title: Change Point Detection with Generative Models
papers.abstract: Change point detection (CPD) methods aim to identify abrupt changes in the properties of time series, which is a key problem in numerous fields. A major class of CPD approaches relies on computing a CPD score, which is either a discrepancy or divergence between two subsequent samples, called windows. A fundamental limitation of window-based CPD is the 'sample size bottleneck.' To ensure temporal precision, windows must be small; however, small samples provide insufficient statistical evidence for the classifiers and deep-learning models currently used to compute CPD scores. This leads to high variance in the scores and frequent mispredictions. Our study tackles this issue by exploring generative models for window augmentation, effectively expanding available data to improve CPD quality. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly enhances CPD. Specifically, we show that this approach allows simple classifiers to outperform complex deep-learning baselines by stabilizing the CPD score distribution.

papers.title: Global Convergence of Second-Order Methods for Physics-Informed Neural Networks in the Overparameterized Limit
papers.abstract: Solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) constitutes a core task in many engineering and scientific disciplines. Physics-informed neural networks and the deep Galerkin method effectively leverage machine learning models to approximate solutions of known PDEs by minimizing residuals corresponding to the PDE operator alongside external constraints. Although second-order optimizers are becoming increasingly popular for training neural networks (NNs) to solve PDEs and empirically outperform their first-order counterparts in both speed and accuracy, the convergence theory for training such models is essentially confined to first-order methods. In this paper, we close this gap and develop a convergence analysis for the regularized Newton and Gauss-Newton methods. As the number of hidden units tends to infinity, the training dynamics converge in probability, with explicit rates, to the solution of a deterministic limit equation involving a Newton neural tangent kernel operator associated with the PDE. Although the limiting kernel operator admits no spectral gap, we prove that, in the overparameterized limit, the PDE residual vanishes as training proceeds, and, under mild assumptions, the NN converges to the PDE solution. We further show that, provided a sufficiently small regularization parameter, the projection of the residual onto any fixed number of leading eigenfunctions decays exponentially fast, demonstrating that this hyperparameter acts as a spectral filter: it lifts the convergence rates of high-frequency components toward those of low-frequency ones, thereby mitigating the spectral bias inherent in gradient descent. Mathematical challenges arise from the implicit parameter update involving a linear system whose dimension increases with the NN width and, for Newton's method, a potentially indefinite Hessian, as well as from the PDE operator entering the kernel.

papers.title: Provably Efficient Offline Discounted Reinforcement Learning under Recursive Entropic Risk
papers.abstract: We study risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in finite discounted infinite-horizon Markov Decision Processes with recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), parameterized by $\beta\neq 0$. We consider both risk-averse ($\beta>0$) and risk-seeking ($\beta<0$) settings. We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent is provided with a fixed dataset and wishes to learn a near-optimal policy using this dataset. We introduce a model-based algorithm, called ERM Value Iteration Lower Confidence Bound (ERM-VI-LCB) and derive a PAC-type bound on its sample complexity. We also establish a corresponding lower bound, demonstrating that exponential dependence on $|\beta|/(1-\gamma)$ asserted by the upper bound is unavoidable in the worst case. The presented bounds provide the first rigorous sample complexity guarantees for offline RL under recursive ERM across both risk-averse and risk-seeking regimes.

papers.title: The Symmetry Budget: How Much Group Structure Should a Network Architecture Assume?
papers.abstract: A network architecture is, in large part, a symmetry assumption: convolution ties weights across translations, attention ties them across permutations, and a fully connected layer ties nothing. When the data are only approximately symmetric, tying trades approximation error against estimation error, and the right amount of tying is a property of the dataset, not of the architecture alone. We study this trade-off in an exactly solvable model: linear maps on signals over the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_d$, with architectures indexed by the subgroup lattice of $\mathbb{Z}_d$, so that a single integer $k \mid d$ interpolates between an unconstrained layer ($k=1$, $d^2$ parameters) and a fully equivariant one ($k=d$, $d$ parameters). We derive the finite-sample excess risk in closed form, show that for a generic symmetry defect the leading-order risk is affine in $1/k$, and prove that intermediate architectures are then never strictly optimal: the lattice collapses to an all-or-nothing choice with phase boundary $n^\star = \sigma^2 d(d-1)/\varepsilon^2$. Structured defects break this collapse and restore interior optima, and we give a closed-form defect profile for a graded defect. Measurements agree with the theory on $60/60$ cells of a $(\varepsilon,n)$ phase diagram and $48/48$ cells of a second phase diagram at $d=16$, recover the predicted exponent as $-1.92$ against $-2$, and exhibit the predicted $k^\star: 12 \to 4 \to 1$ ladder under graded defects; a two-layer nonlinear control reproduces the crossover. We also characterize when the affine collapse survives for non-abelian groups.

papers.title: A Causal Energy Prior for Learning Directed Acyclic Graphs
papers.abstract: Bayesian learning of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) has long relied on non- or weakly informative priors, on the assumption that the information needed for an informative one is rarely available. In genetics and systems biology, annotation databases now make it possible to assemble a prior DAG before learning from data. Existing informative priors are local: they score a DAG arc by arc and cannot encode how interventions propagate along its paths. Thus, we propose the local-global energy prior (LGE), a Gibbs distribution over DAGs whose energy combines a local divergence from the prior DAG, the Structural Hamming Distance, and a causal one, the Structural Intervention Distance. We derive rules to calibrate its decay and the weight of the two divergences from the prior DAG alone. We quantify how much prior mass stays on the true DAG, and how much data overturn the prior, when the prior DAG is partially incorrect. In simulations, LGE improves both the structural accuracy of maximum a posteriori DAGs and the fit of the corresponding Bayesian networks to the true distribution over non- and weakly informative priors, even when half of the arcs of the prior DAG are wrong. We also showcase LGE on a gene regulatory network learned from single-cell kidney data.

papers.title: Evaluating Ensemble Methods for Algorithmic Stability Under Data Perturbations
papers.abstract: Standard classification algorithms often exhibit sensitivity near decision boundaries, which can compound instability that already exists from overfitting to a subset of high-influence samples. Ensembling is commonly used to stabilize classifiers, but we show that it can destabilize those that are already stable. The well-established practice of subbagging can yield substantial improvements in stability, as we validate in the cause-of-death classification setting. However, its effect depends on the perturbation level, and for stable classifiers the finite number of bags introduces destabilizing Monte Carlo noise that shrinks only slowly as the number of bags grows. This instability can be mitigated, though, by the recently proposed inflated argmax, which allows for multi-class predictions in ambiguous cases. We further examine the extent to which the Rashomon set, the collection of distinct models that achieve near-optimal predictive performance, can reduce instability by leveraging predictive multiplicity rather than resampling. We find that the Rashomon ensemble can stabilize unstable classifiers, but requires sufficient predictive multiplicity, which is not guaranteed. It is a promising direction, but not currently a general substitute for subbagging. Our results are consistent with an influence equalization interpretation of why these ensemble approaches stabilize unstable classifiers, although their failures on stable classifiers appear to have distinct sources.

papers.title: Gaussian priors from nonlinear PDEs with the semiclassical approximation
papers.abstract: Probabilistic numerical methods for partial differential equations (PDE) combines the governing physics with observations to treat solving the PDE as a Bayesian inverse problem. This allows techniques to quantify the uncertainty in the field reconstruction under model-form error. In the majority of cases, a Gaussian prior is assigned to the field of interest, and Bayes's theorem in the infinite-dimensional setting is used to derive the posterior. While Gaussians have been shown to be well-suited for linear PDEs, a similar treatment for nonlinear PDEs remains open-ended. In this work, study the use of the semiclassical approximation to construct Gaussian priors from variational energies or integrated square residuals for probabilistic numerics. The prior is derived by expanding the PDE energy about a stable solution and uncovering a Gaussian form. We then analyze the different characteristics of the resulting priors as they pertain to the inverse problem. In particular, we find that the covariance operator is given by the inverse of the Hessian of the energy whose associated Cameron-Martin space is the solution space of the PDE. We also find that the prior responds to model-form error by sharpening or flattening itself depending on the distance between the ground truth and the solution of the assumed model.

papers.title: Centered Kernel Distance: Dimension-Free Error Bounds for Comparing Neural Representations
papers.abstract: The asymptotic error of representational similarity metrics such as centered kernel alignment (CKA) and representational similarity analysis (RSA) has been well-characterized, but there are no realistic bounds on how estimates of representational similarity $\textit{simultaneously}$ depend on the number of sampled neurons ($N$) and experimental conditions ($M$). We study the natural metric counterpart of CKA and RSA, which we call the Centered Kernel Distance (CKD). We show that CKD admits an unbiased estimator, whereas several popular similarity measures including CKA have no unbiased estimator. Under mild assumptions, we show that estimation error of CKD decays in proportion to $1/M + 1/N$. Strikingly, the rate in this bound does not depend on the dimensionality of the space of experimental conditions. Thus, similarity estimation does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality, which plagues similar problems in high-dimensional statistics. We verify our results empirically in random shallow neural networks, trained neural networks, and macaque visual cortex data. Ultimately, this paper advances a framework for predicting the error of similarity estimators in experiments by relaxing existing, biologically-unrealistic assumptions. Our theoretical and empirical predictions produce specific prescriptions on how to most efficiently estimate the similarity between multiple neural systems.

papers.title: On the Impact of Extra Information in Bandit Learning: More is Not Always Merrier
papers.abstract: More data is commonly assumed to improve learning performance, however, we show that this intuition can surprisngly fail in sequential decision-making. Considering a stochastic bandits setup with exogenous extra information, we ask if the free and unbiased extra reward samples are guaranteed to reduce the regret of the learner. We introduce a formal notion of `non-degradation under extra information' and demonstrate that the widely used Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB) violates this property, i.e., there exist benign extra-information under which UCB incurs strictly higher regret than when run without extra information. We contrast this behaviour with Thompson Sampling and Explore-Then-Commit, which appear to benefit from the same extra information. Constructively, we propose a meta-algorithm that provably enforces non-degradation for a broad class of bandit algorithms. We also run empirical simulations to study our meta-algorithm.

papers.title: Adversarial Bandit Convex Optimization with $d^{3/2}\sqrt{n}$ Regret
papers.abstract: We study adversarial bandit convex optimization, where in each of $n$ rounds a learner chooses a point $A_t$ in a convex body $\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ and observes only a noisy value of a convex loss $f_t:\mathcal{K}\to[0,1]$ at that point. The losses are chosen by an adversary, who may change them from round to round and adapt them to the learner's past actions. We improve the best known regret bound for this problem from $\widetilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt n)$ (Lattimore, 2020, 2026) to $\widetilde O(d^{3/2}\sqrt n)$, which matches the rate conjectured by Bubeck et al. (2017). Together with the recent lower bound of $\Omega(d^{4/3}\sqrt n)$ due to Rajaraman and Han (2026), it determines the minimax regret up to a factor of $d^{1/6}$ and logarithmic factors. The algorithm is an online Newton step with Gaussian exploration. Unlike earlier methods of this kind, it uses unbiased estimates of the gradient and Hessian of the Gaussian smoothing of the loss, rather than of an optimistic surrogate.

papers.title: Improved Sample Complexity of Robust Reinforcement Learning with KL Uncertainty Sets
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study distributionally robust reinforcement learning with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets. The goal is to find a policy that maximizes the robust value function, defined as the worst-case value over all transition kernels in the uncertainty set. Assuming access to a generative model, we aim to understand the sample complexity of finding an $\epsilon$-optimal robust policy. The best-known sample complexity results in the literature show a non-trivial gap of $\mathcal{O}\{\max\{p_\wedge^{-1}(1-\gamma)^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-2}\}\}$ between the upper and lower bounds, where $p_\wedge$ denotes the minimum positive transition probability of the nominal transition kernel, and $\gamma$ is the discount factor. More importantly, existing results on the lower bound only cover a limited range of the uncertainty level. In this paper, we develop tighter and complete upper and lower bounds for robust RL with KL-defined uncertainty sets. Our upper bound is the tightest among all existing studies, and it improves upon the best-known bound by at least the order of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{p_\wedge^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-1}\})$ for uncertainty level $\delta\in(0,1)$. Furthermore, our lower bound holds for any uncertainty level. Our upper and lower bounds (nearly) match in various regimes, providing improved results for this problem.

papers.title: Understanding Double Descent through Universal Compression
papers.abstract: Many deep learning models exhibit a double-descent phenomenon, where test loss exhibits a sharp peak near the interpolation threshold and then descends a second time as model size grows further, contrary to the U-shape predicted by the classical bias--variance tradeoff. The double-descent phenomenon has been found and explained in toy classical models, but is not well-understood in modern deep learning despite extensive empirical study. We interpret double descent through the novel lens of universal compression. Specifically, we upper bound the maximum-likelihood excess test loss as a sum of four terms: an approximation-and-shift term, a minimax batch regret, a prior cost, and an MLE-vs-Bayes gap. Under exact posterior sampling, we further show that the expected MLE-vs-ensemble gap lower-bounds the MLE-vs-Bayes gap in the well-specified setting. In our experiments, a Gaussian-prior SGLD approximation to the Bayes predictor, unlike SGD, shows no pronounced interpolation peak. Experiments with uniform random labels support this gap as a major contributor to the double-descent peak; here, the SGD cross-entropy is roughly four times the SGLD ensemble cross-entropy at the peak, while the ensemble cross-entropy remains near $\log 10$.

papers.title: RHOPE: LLM-Augmented Adaptive Experimental Design with Complex Contextual Information
papers.abstract: Experimental design allocates limited measurement effort across candidate treatments to learn their expected outcomes. Adaptive designs refine allocations as evidence accumulates, improving estimation and treatment selection. Contextual information can inform these decisions, but exploiting unstructured or high-dimensional context remains challenging. We use large language models (LLMs) to transform complex context into proxy outcomes and propose Residual Horizon Optimization for Prediction-Powered Experimentation (RHOPE), a principled Bayesian adaptive experimentation framework that combines true outcomes with LLM-generated proxy outcomes and formulates finite-batch design as a posterior Markov decision process (MDP). Our methodology uses proxy outcomes in two ways: sample augmentation improves estimation precision, while observing proxies before each allocation decision provides advance information. Synthetic experiments and semi-synthetic experiments using Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) data suggest that estimation precision drives most gains, with smaller advance-information gains, and highlight the importance of proxy informativeness and moment-estimation accuracy.

papers.title: A Graphical Criterion for Linear Causal Bounds
papers.abstract: The values of causal effects and counterfactuals are typically only partially identified from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounding. With discretely-valued variables, under certain conditions, sharp bounds can be derived by solving one linear program. This is then computationally tractable for many causal questions. In this paper, for every diagram in which each confounded component has at most two hidden causes, we give necessary and sufficient conditions for the sharp bounds to be equal to the optimum of one linear program for every (positive) input probability table. This algorithm is implemented in a new Python package, called "partialid", that allows users to compose assumptions, queries, and data to obtain sharp bounds in a computationally tractable manner.

papers.title: Accelerated Proximal Gradient Methods for Multiobjective Optimization over Probability Measures via Hilbert-Space Lifting
papers.abstract: Many sampling and inference tasks require a single distribution that balances several targets. We formulate this task as multiobjective optimization of Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences over probability measures, in the Pareto sense. The particle method MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2025) uses explicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version A-MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2026) lacks discrete-time guarantees. We propose the multiobjective Wasserstein proximal gradient (MWPG), which uses implicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version, multiobjective Wasserstein accelerated proximal gradient (MWAPG), with rigorous discrete-time guarantees. Our key idea is a Hilbert-space lifting: each measure is represented as the pushforward of a fixed base measure by a map in a Hilbert space. The problem then becomes a constrained multiobjective composite problem over transport maps, to which accelerated proximal gradient methods apply. For convex and smooth potentials, we show that MWAPG decreases a Pareto merit function at the rate $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$; for $m$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth potentials, the rate is $\mathcal{O}\big((1-\sqrt{m/L})^k\big)$. We also give closed-form Gaussian updates and particle implementations based on input-convex neural networks, which require no score estimation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world dataset show that MWAPG needs far fewer iterations than MWPG and matches or outperforms A-MWGraD in Bayesian multi-task learning.

papers.title: Conditional Independence Graph Learning from Dependent Data Via Time-Delay Embedding
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of inferring the conditional independence graph (CIG) of a high-dimensional stationary multivariate Gaussian time series which could be short-range dependent (SRD) or long-range dependent (LRD). In a time series graph, each component of the vector series is represented by a distinct node, and associations between components are represented by edges between the corresponding nodes. We consider a time-domain approach based on time-delay embedding, casting the problem as one of multi-attribute graph estimation for random vectors where a vector is associated with each node of the graph. For an embedding dimension $d$, at each node the associated $(d+1)$-dimensional random vector consists of a time series component and its $d$ delayed copies, with integer delays up to $d \ge 1$. Graph estimation from dependent data has been investigated in the past using frequency-domain methods whose analysis is restricted to SRD data. We consider a penalized negative pseudo log-likelihood function with convex lasso or non-convex regularizations to estimate the CIG. Non-convex regularization functions are log-sum, smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) and minimax concave penalty (MCP). We exploit an existing alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) approach to optimize the objective function. We establish sufficient conditions in a high-dimensional setting for consistency, local convexity when using non-convex penalties, and graph recovery, for both SRD and LRD series. We illustrate our approach with both synthetic and real-data examples. For a $p$-dimensional time series, the computational complexity of the ADMM algorithm is ${\cal O}((d+1)^3 p^3)$. Based on the numerical examples, a heuristic is suggested and illustrated for selection of $d$ which, in theory, should tend to infinity to infer the time series graph.

papers.title: Local structural transfer learning of non-Gaussian DAG and its application to multi-source cancer gene regulatory networks
papers.abstract: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) is pivotal for modeling gene regulatory networks in cancer pathogenesis, yet single-study genomic data is often limited for accurate DAG reconstruction. Although multi-source datasets provide augmented sample sizes, substantial heterogeneity persists across real-world cohorts. It remains an open question how to pool the heterogeneous data with only local similarity together for better DAG structure reconstruction in the target study. In this paper, we introduce a novel set of structural similarity measures for DAGs and then present a transfer DAG learning framework by effectively leveraging information from auxiliary DAGs with node-level local similarities. Our theoretical analysis shows substantial improvement in terms of DAG reconstruction in the target study, which is in sharp contrast to most existing transfer learning methods requiring global similarity. The advantage of the proposed transfer DAG learning is also supported by extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic data and multi-source cancer genomics data.

papers.title: Stability Regularized Cross-Validation
papers.abstract: We study hyperparameter selection via cross-validation, motivated by settings in which the selected $k$-fold cross-validation error underestimates the selected model's test error. We propose a nested $k$-fold cross-validation scheme that minimizes a weighted sum of the standard cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, with the stability weight selected by an outer cross-validation loop. We derive a generalization bound that controls test error using the cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, together with correction terms common to every candidate. In a stylized ridge regression setting, we then show that whether the stability weight improves expected test-set performance depends on the signal-to-noise ratio, with the greatest improvement when the signal-to-noise ratio is small. On $13$ real-world regression datasets, the procedure reduces the average out-of-sample MSE relative to $k$-fold cross-validation by $5.6\%$ for sparse regression and by $6.8\%$ for CART. A side benefit of an outer cross-validation loop is that the selected error estimates are better calibrated than those from ordinary $k$-fold cross-validation: the error estimate moves from 12.3\% below the selected test-set MSE to 5.8\% above it for sparse regression and from 10.3\% below to 0.2\% above it for CART.
